claims.text: A DFT-plus-machine-learning framework will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity more accurately than conventional analytical models based on pristine crystals.
Including defect and impurity scattering in the framework will improve conductivity predictions.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen produces defects that alter electron scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Impurity scattering predominates in HfNbTaTiZr over approximately 0–200 K.
Phonon scattering is influential over 300–1200 K and is modified by oxygen.
Experimental conductivity data are available in the two targeted temperature ranges for HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Representative defect structures and oxygen substitution sites can be incorporated into DFT calculations for this alloy.
The machine-learning component will be trained on limited experimental conductivity data from the targeted temperature ranges.
Oxygen-induced defects, vacancies, and realistic microstructural disorder provide a structural basis for altered electron scattering.
Oxygen substitutions and associated lattice distortions create enhanced electron scattering that defect-free models neglect.
Machine-learning calibration against conductivity measurements will correct systematic predictive deviations.
The hybrid framework will reduce predictive discrepancy by approximately 20–30% relative to conventional analytical predictions.
In the 0–200 K regime, the framework will predict lower conductivity because of enhanced impurity scattering.
In the 300–1200 K regime, the framework will more accurately capture the interplay between phonon and defect scattering.
Conventional analytical or DFT predictions use fully ordered, defect-free crystal models that omit oxygen impurities and microstructural disorder.
Such conventional predictions typically disagree with experimental conductivity data.
The claimed improvement applies within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K and to samples containing no more than about 1 wt.% oxygen.
Extension to substantially different compositions, higher oxygen concentrations, or other defect types would require further refinement.
The hypothesis is falsified if held-out error is not reduced by at least 20% relative to the conventional defect-free model.
The hypothesis is also rejected if predicted conductivity differs from measurement by more than 20% at any critical temperature.
